questions.scenario: A Standard Edition account has a table with DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 1 and MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS left at its default. A stream on the table feeds a task. The task was suspended after repeated failures and nobody consumed the stream for 9 days. The stream holds unconsumed changes. An engineer now runs SHOW STREAMS and finds that STALE is FALSE.
questions.stem: Which statement explains this result and its cost?

options.text: The stream is not stale only because the retention of 1 day was reset each day by SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA calls on the stream.
Snowflake extended the table's retention to the stream's offset, up to MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS (default 14 days), and the extra retained history adds storage cost.
The extension applies only to Enterprise Edition or higher, so the Standard Edition stream must have been consumed by another process.
The stream is stale after 1 day, and SHOW STREAMS reports a stale stream as FALSE until the next query reads it.

explanation.correct: When a stream is not consumed, Snowflake extends the source table's data retention to the stream's offset, up to MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS, which defaults to 14 days. This applies regardless of edition and the extra retained history costs storage. Here 9 days is inside the 14-day window.

distractors.A: SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA prevents staleness only when the stream is empty and the function returns FALSE. This stream holds unconsumed changes, and nothing in the scenario calls the function.
distractors.C: The retention extension applies regardless of edition. Nothing needs to have consumed the stream.
distractors.D: SHOW STREAMS reports staleness directly through the STALE and STALE_AFTER columns. It doesn't wait for a query to mark a stream stale.

questions.scenario: A stream s_orders is defined on table orders and holds 100 unconsumed change rows. An engineer runs BEGIN; INSERT INTO audit_a SELECT * FROM s_orders; INSERT INTO audit_b SELECT * FROM s_orders; COMMIT;. After the transaction starts but before the first INSERT runs, another session inserts 20 new rows into orders and commits.
questions.stem: What happens when the transaction commits?

options.text: audit_a gets 100 rows and audit_b gets 0 rows, because the first INSERT moved the stream offset.
audit_a gets 100 rows and audit_b gets 120 rows, because tables and streams use read committed isolation.
audit_a and audit_b each get the same 100 rows, and the 20 new rows stay in the stream for the next consumption.
audit_a and audit_b each get 120 rows, because a stream is read as of the time each statement runs.

explanation.correct: Streams use repeatable read isolation. Within a transaction, every statement sees the stream as of the transaction start. The DML consumes the records only if the transaction commits, and changes committed by other transactions in the meantime appear after it.

distractors.A: The offset moves only when the transaction that uses the stream commits, not at the first INSERT. Both statements see the same records.
distractors.B: Tables use read committed isolation but streams use repeatable read. The two statements can't see different record sets.
distractors.D: A stream queried in an explicit transaction is read as of the transaction start, not the statement time, so the 20 later rows are excluded.

questions.scenario: A team wants a task that loads rows from the stream s_events into a target table only when the stream has data. They want no polling schedule and no compute spent until changes arrive. They also want Snowflake to manage the compute, so no warehouse is named.
questions.stem: Which task definition meets these requirements?

options.text: CREATE TASK t TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL = '15 MINUTES' WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('s_events') AS INSERT INTO tgt SELECT * FROM s_events;
CREATE TASK t WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('s_events') AS INSERT INTO tgt SELECT * FROM s_events;
CREATE TASK t WAREHOUSE = etl_wh WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('s_events') AS INSERT INTO tgt SELECT * FROM s_events;
CREATE TASK t SCHEDULE = '1 MINUTE' TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL = '15 MINUTES' WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('s_events') AS INSERT INTO tgt SELECT * FROM s_events;

explanation.correct: A triggered task has a WHEN clause on the stream and no SCHEDULE. A serverless triggered task omits WAREHOUSE and must set TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL.

distractors.B: A serverless triggered task requires TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL. Without it, and without a warehouse, the definition is incomplete.
distractors.C: Naming a warehouse makes this a user-managed triggered task. The requirement was for Snowflake-managed compute.
distractors.D: Adding SCHEDULE turns this into a scheduled task that checks the condition every minute and skips when empty. It is not event-triggered.

questions.scenario: A scheduled task graph has a root task and five child tasks. The fourth task in the chain fails at 02:10 after the first three have succeeded. The nightly run cannot wait for the next schedule. The team wants to rerun only the failed part of that run, without rerunning the tasks that already succeeded.

options.text: Run EXECUTE TASK on the root task with no extra clause.
Set TASK_AUTO_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 1 on the failed child task and wait.
Run EXECUTE TASK on the root task with RETRY LAST.
Run ALTER TASK on the failed child to RESUME it, which reruns it.

explanation.correct: EXECUTE TASK ... RETRY LAST reruns from the last failed task or tasks in the latest graph run, as a new run with the attempt number increased by one.

distractors.A: A plain EXECUTE TASK on the root starts a new full run of the graph, including the tasks that already succeeded.
distractors.B: TASK_AUTO_RETRY_ATTEMPTS is set on the root, and when a child fails it retries the whole graph. It doesn't apply retroactively to the failed run.
distractors.D: RESUME changes the task's state and doesn't rerun it. The graph version is set when the root is resumed or executed.

questions.scenario: A data engineer owns several views and their underlying tables and has enabled change tracking on all of them. The engineer wants to create a stream on views that meet the requirements for streams on views.
questions.stem: Which TWO views can have a stream created on them? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A view that aggregates order totals per customer with GROUP BY
A view that returns SELECT DISTINCT customer_id from a table
A view that inner joins orders to customers and filters on region
A view defined over an external table
A view that combines two tables with UNION ALL

explanation.correct: A stream on a view allows projections, filters, inner or cross joins, and UNION ALL.

distractors.A: GROUP BY is not allowed in a view that has a stream.
distractors.B: DISTINCT is not allowed in a view that has a stream.
distractors.D: Views over external tables and directory tables are not supported for streams.

questions.scenario: A pipeline reads files that land in an S3 bucket through an external table. The team wants a stream on the external table to drive a downstream load. Files are sometimes removed from the bucket by a lifecycle rule, and those removals must not appear as deleted rows in the stream.
questions.stem: Which statement creates a stream that works for this external table?

options.text: CREATE STREAM s ON EXTERNAL TABLE ext_t;
CREATE STREAM s ON EXTERNAL TABLE ext_t APPEND_ONLY = TRUE;
CREATE STREAM s ON EXTERNAL TABLE ext_t SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS = TRUE;
CREATE STREAM s ON EXTERNAL TABLE ext_t INSERT_ONLY = TRUE;

explanation.correct: Streams on external tables must be insert-only. An insert-only stream records inserts only, so a file removed from cloud storage is not recorded as a delete.

distractors.A: A default stream is a standard stream, which also records deletes. External tables require INSERT_ONLY = TRUE.
distractors.B: APPEND_ONLY applies to standard tables, dynamic tables, Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables and views. External tables use INSERT_ONLY instead.
distractors.C: SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS only changes what the first consumption returns. It doesn't make the stream insert-only, so the stream type is still invalid for an external table.

questions.scenario: A table holds GPS pings in a GEOGRAPHY column. Rows are only ever inserted, and the table is truncated every night right after the load task consumes the new rows. A standard stream on this table does not return change data for the geospatial data. The team wants the cheapest stream that works.

options.text: A standard stream created with SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS = TRUE
A stream created with APPEND_ONLY = TRUE
A stream created with INSERT_ONLY = TRUE
A standard stream created AT (OFFSET => -3600)

explanation.correct: Standard streams can't return change data for geospatial data, so an append-only stream is used. It records inserts only, is faster than a standard stream, and lets the source be truncated right after consumption without extra cost for the next query.

distractors.A: SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS affects only the first consumption. The stream is still a standard stream and still can't return geospatial change data.
distractors.C: INSERT_ONLY is for external tables and externally managed Iceberg tables, and for some Delta Direct tables. It is not the option for a standard table.
distractors.D: AT (OFFSET => ...) sets where the stream starts with Time Travel. It doesn't change the stream type.

questions.scenario: A deployment script runs CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM s_orders ON TABLE orders every release. The stream usually has unconsumed changes when the script runs. The team wants the replaced stream to keep the current offset, so that no pending changes are lost.

options.text: CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM s_orders ON TABLE orders AT (STREAM => 's_orders');
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM s_orders ON TABLE orders COPY GRANTS;
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM s_orders ON TABLE orders SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS = TRUE;
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM s_orders ON TABLE orders;

explanation.correct: AT (STREAM => 'name') starts the new stream at the same offset as the named stream. With OR REPLACE it keeps the current offset when the stream is recreated.

distractors.B: COPY GRANTS keeps the privileges, except OWNERSHIP. It doesn't carry over the offset.
distractors.C: SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS makes the first consumption return all rows that existed at creation, which would reprocess data that was already consumed.
distractors.D: A plain CREATE OR REPLACE starts a new stream at the current point. CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM is also a way to advance the offset without using the changes, so unconsumed changes are lost.

questions.scenario: The table sales is owned by role DATA_OWNER. Change tracking has never been enabled on it and no stream exists on it. Role ETL_ROLE has CREATE STREAM on the schema, USAGE on the database and schema, and SELECT on sales. When ETL_ROLE runs CREATE STREAM s_sales ON TABLE sales, the statement fails.

options.text: ETL_ROLE also needs OPERATE on the table before it can create a stream.
ETL_ROLE needs USAGE on a warehouse, because creating a stream starts the change tracking job.
Change tracking isn't enabled yet, and only the table owner can create the first stream on the table. DATA_OWNER can create it.
A stream can't be created on a table unless the creator role owns the schema.

explanation.correct: If change tracking isn't yet enabled on the table, only the table owner can create the first stream. Creating that stream enables change tracking.

distractors.A: OPERATE on a table is not a stream creation requirement. Creating a stream needs CREATE STREAM on the schema and SELECT on the source.
distractors.B: A warehouse is billed only when the stream is queried. The object itself has no charge, and a warehouse isn't a creation requirement.
distractors.D: The creator needs CREATE STREAM on the schema and some privilege on the database and schema, not ownership of the schema.

questions.scenario: A team is moving several tasks to serverless compute and reviewing how serverless sizing and the related parameters behave.
questions.stem: Which THREE statements about serverless tasks are correct? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Serverless sizing history is discarded on suspend, so a resumed task starts again from its initial size.
USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE defaults to MEDIUM and is ignored after a few successful runs.
USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE can be set together with WAREHOUSE to size the first run on that warehouse.
TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL has no effect once the task is already running at its maximum size.
Serverless tasks are the right choice for workloads larger than XXLARGE.
The maximum serverless size is XXLARGE, and SERVERLESS_TASK_MAX_STATEMENT_SIZE defaults to XXLARGE.

explanation.correct: The initial size parameter defaults to MEDIUM and stops mattering after a few successful runs. TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL is ignored once the task is at maximum size. The serverless maximum is XXLARGE, which is also the default of the max-size bound.

distractors.A: Serverless sizing history is kept across suspend and resume. It is removed only when the task is recreated with CREATE OR REPLACE.
distractors.C: Setting USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE together with WAREHOUSE is an error. The parameter applies only to serverless tasks.
distractors.E: Workloads larger than XXLARGE are a case for a user-managed warehouse, because serverless tops out at XXLARGE.
